Gower Abstract Quasi-Newton (QN) methods have long been among the most effective methods for large-scale unconstrained convex optimization. Two obstacles have limited their use in deep learning: non-convexity and enormous parameter sizes. We introduce SoftServe , a family of QN methods designed to overcome these obstacles without line searches or ad hoc curvature corrections. SoftServe derives positive-definite curvature estimates from the variational objective of Berglund et al. (2025) , even in the presence of negative curvature. We develop diagonal and Kronecker-factored variants that preserve positive definiteness by construction and scale to massive neural networks. Finally, SoftServe relies on the stable coupled Newton–Schulz iteration for the required matrix operations, replacing costly matrix decompositions with GPU-friendly matrix multiplications. SoftServe excels on problems that are severely ill-conditioned, including tasks such as recurrent networks, deep autoencoders, physics-informed neural networks, and a 136M-parameter physics-informed diffusion model, often achieving lower losses than established baselines including Adam, Muon, and SOAP. 2 2 footnotetext: Work done while at the Flatiron Institute. Email: joohwanko@cs.umass.edu . 3 3 footnotetext: Equal senior authors. 1 Introduction Quasi-Newton methods, such as the celebrated BFGS method ( Broyden, 1970 ; Fletcher, 1970 ; Goldfarb, 1970 ; Shanno, 1970 ) , are among the most effective methods for large-scale, convex deterministic optimization. Deep learning has led to renewed interest in adapting these methods to train large networks ( Goldfarb et al., 2020 ; Ren et al., 2022 ) . However, applying these methods to deep learning requires curvature estimates that can accommodate non-convex objectives and gradient noise while remaining computationally efficient. To see how curvature enters the optimization update, consider a generic second-order method. For parameters x ∈ ℝ D x\in\mathbb{R}^{D} , second-order methods typically take steps of the form x + = x − γ ​ 𝑯 ​ g . x^{+}=x-\gamma m{H}g. Here x + x^{+} is the updated parameter vector, and γ > 0 \gamma>0 is the step size. The vector g ∈ ℝ D g\in\mathbb{R}^{D} is the (stochastic) gradient at x x , and the matrix 𝑯 ∈ ℝ D × D  m{H}\in\mathbb{R}^{D	imes D} is an estimate of the inverse Hessian. Non-convexity of the objective poses a fundamental challenge for second-order optimization methods because the true Hessian could have negative eigenvalues. If the estimate 𝑯  m{H} has a negative eigenvalue, then the update direction − 𝑯 ​ g - m{H}g could be an ascent direction, which would increase the loss function. This is one of the reasons why first-order methods are often preferred in deep learning: one can always guarantee descent (in expectation). For a second-order method to be applicable in deep learning, the estimate 𝑯  m{H} must always be positive definite, even in the presence of directions of negative curvature. For quasi-Newton methods, such as BFGS, maintaining positive definiteness is at odds with the main tool used to measure curvature, namely the secant equation . In the presence of negative curvature, enforcing the secant equation can inadvertently force the Hessian estimate to become indefinite, as we will show in Section 2 . The standard remedy is to use sophisticated line search procedures to only move in directions of positive curvature ( Nocedal and Wright, 2006 ; Wolfe, 1969 ) . But these line searches require access to the full batch loss, which is too costly and not feasible in the stochastic setting of deep learning. Beyond the challenges arising from non-convexity and stochastic objectives, the sheer scale of modern deep learning models makes storing and updating dense curvature estimates prohibitively expensive. A standard approach for reducing this cost is the limited memory approach of L-BFGS ( Liu and Nocedal, 1989 ) , which typically uses only 10 pairs of parameter and gradient differences to implicitly build the estimate 𝑯  m{H} . But storing 10 pairs of parameters and gradients would require storing 10 copies of our model and 10 copies of the gradient, increasing the memory storage by 20-fold. This is infeasible for all but small models. To scale to modern deep learning, it is common to approximate the matrix 𝑯  m{H} by a diagonal matrix ( Duchi et al., 2011 ; Tieleman and Hinton, 2012 ; Kingma and Ba, 2015 ) or a Kronecker-structured matrix ( Martens and Grosse, 2015 ; Gupta et al., 2018 ) . For quasi-Newton optimization, while Kronecker-structured updates have been proposed for applying BFGS to deep learning ( Goldfarb et al., 2020 ; Ren et al., 2022 ) , this approach still needs to be applied with mechanisms for handling non-convexity and stochasticity, limiting its applicability. A promising new direction is to reconsider how curvature enters the quasi-Newton update. Recently, Berglund et al. (2025) show that by replacing the secant equation with a soft secant penalty we can ensure that our Hessian estimate is positive definite, even in the presence of negative curvature. But Berglund et al. (2025) only consider dense estimates, making their approach infeasible for deep learning. We introduce SoftServe (Soft S ecant E quation R egularized with V ariational E ntropy), a quasi-Newton framework that combines the flexibility of a soft secant constraint ( Li, 2019 ; Berglund et al., 2025 ) with the computational advantages of a structured matrix approximation of the inverse Hessian. Optimizing within diagonal and Kronecker-structured families yields novel updates that preserve positive definiteness, without full batch evaluations or line searches. We develop efficient algorithms for computing these updates using modern GPU-friendly numerical linear algebra methods, such as variants of Newton-Schulz ( Amsel et al., 2026 ; Higham, 2008 ) , allowing SoftServe to scale to large neural networks. We then demonstrate the utility of SoftServe on several deep learning tasks where curvature information is fundamental—such as severely ill-conditioned tasks—including recurrent networks, autoencoders, and physics-informed models (such as a 136M-parameter diffusion model). On these tasks we find that SoftServe often outperforms modern methods such as Adam, Muon, and SOAP. A Python implementation of SoftServe is available at https://github.com/joohwanko/SoftServe . 2 Quasi-Newton Preliminaries Here we introduce our notation and review important quasi-Newton (QN) ideas that are relevant to SoftServe . For simplicity, in this section we represent all parameters as a flattened vector x ∈ ℝ D x\in\mathbb{R}^{D} . Install · Quick start · Examples · Experiments · Citation SoftServe learns positive-definite, structured inverse-curvature estimates from secant pairs. This repository provides Kronecker ( SoftServeKron ) and diagonal ( SoftServeDiag ) optimizers, experiment runners, and selected paper configurations. Installation Tested with Python 3.12 and PyTorch 2.13.0. With uv : git clone https://github.com/joohwanko/SoftServe.git cd SoftServe uv venv --python 3.12 source .venv/bin/activate uv pip install -e . Use pip instead From the repository root: python3.12 -m venv .venv source .venv/bin/activate python -m pip install -e . Quick start from softserve import SoftServeKron optimizer = SoftServeKron ( model , lr = 1e-3 , lam = 99 , K = 10 , fallback = "adamw" , fallback_lr = 3e-4 , ) Pass the model , after moving it to its training device. SoftServe routes matrix weights and convolution kernels to Kron, and biases, embeddings, normalization parameters, and other tensors to the fallback. Matrix factors are bounded to blocks of at most 256 × 256. Choose fallback="adam" , "adamw" , or "softserve-diag" (default). fallback_lr defaults to lr . Diag shares Kron's λ, momentum, and refresh interval; Adam/AdamW use independent fallback_betas=(0.9, 0.999) and fallback_weight_decay=0 . Set weight decay explicitly when wanted. Defaults are beta1=0.9 , no Nesterov, and constrained normalization. Kron uses Gram QME with 18 root and 10 inverse iterations. SoftServeDiag(model, lr=..., lam=..., K=10) applies the diagonal method to every trainable parameter. Examples Both loops use this small regression problem. Run the setup afresh before either loop. import torch from torch import nn from softserve import SoftServeKron torch . manual_seed ( 0 ) x = torch . randn ( 256 , 8 ) y = x [:, : 1 ] - 0.5 * x [:, 1 : 2 ] model = nn . Sequential ( nn . Linear ( 8 , 32 ), nn . Tanh (), nn . Linear ( 32 , 1 ) ) loss_fn = nn . MSELoss () optimizer = SoftServeKron ( model , lr = 1e-2 , lam = 99 , K = 10 , fallback = "adam" , fallback_lr = 1e-3 , ) Deterministic: fixed data For a fixed, deterministic objective, step() reuses gradients from the training loop. Curvature is refreshed after each K updates, when the next gradient becomes available. No extra backward pass is needed. Use the closure version below if data, randomness, or forward-pass state changes. for _ in range ( 100 ): optimizer . zero_grad ( set_to_none = True ) loss = loss_fn ( model ( x ), y ) loss . backward () optimizer . step () Stochastic: new minibatches Sample a minibatch outside the closure. Bind it in the closure's default arguments so it remains available for replay. step(closure) does the usual training backward pass and, every K updates, one extra backward pass on the interval's starting minibatch. for _ in range ( 100 ): indices = torch . randint ( len ( x ), ( 64 ,)) xb , yb = x [ indices ], y [ indices ] def closure ( xb = xb , yb = yb ): optimizer . zero_grad ( set_to_none = True ) loss = loss_fn ( model ( xb ), yb ) loss . backward () return loss optimizer . step ( closure ) At K=10 , 100 updates use 110 backward passes. Parameter/gradient snapshots and replay are handled internally. Replay restores the starting randomness and registered model buffers, including standard Dropout and BatchNorm, without advancing their current state a second time. Checkpointing and supported usage Save stochastic checkpoints when optimizer.checkpoint_ready is true, normally after a multiple of K updates. state_dict() refuses to save an unfinished interval because a Python closure cannot be serialized. Deterministic checkpoints can be saved at any step. Save the model, scheduler, data position, and RNG state as usual for exact training resumption. Keep the captured batch and loss settings unchanged until replay finishes. Closures should only zero gradients, evaluate the loss, and call backward() ; do not advance a data loader or scheduler inside them. Custom RNG generators or mutable state outside registered model buffers need explicit integration. Use max_grad_norm=1.0 if clipping is needed; it clips updates' gradients while retaining raw gradients for secants. LR schedulers act on both parameter groups. optimizer.routing shows the parameter assignment. Supported: dense FP32/FP64 parameters on one CPU or CUDA device, including tied weights. Autocast is supported; GradScaler, sparse gradients, DataParallel/DDP/FSDP, and changing model parameters/devices after construction are not supported by this interface. The original SoftServeKron(parameters, ...) , parameter_step() , and update_curvature() interfaces remain unchanged. Paper runners retain their explicit, task-specific routing and replay; K belongs to the new model interface, not the legacy T option. Experiments Install the experiment dependencies, list the selected configurations, and run one: uv pip install -e ' .[experiments,soap] ' python run.py --config configs/rnn.json --list python run.py --config configs/rnn.json --index 0 --seed 1 Configs cover RNN Adding, MNIST, small PINNs, PIDM, and GPT; see configs/ . RNN runs on CPU; the other tasks use GPUs. PirateNet provides configurations only , pending redistribution permission ( details ). Use --lr to tune on seed 0, then run the evaluation seeds listed in each config. Use --set KEY=JSON for other overrides. Results go to outputs/ ; keep sweeps and final runs in separate directories. Data preparation and reproduction notes RNN and small PINNs generate data locally. For the other tasks: python prepare.py mnist uv pip install -r requirements-pidm.txt python prepare.py pidm # ~5.3 GB download python prepare.py fineweb FineWeb preparation processes 2.01B tokens to preserve the validation split, although training uses 200M. Compatible train.bin and val.bin files can instead be placed in data/fineweb/ . The historical dataset revision was not recorded; use --revision to pin new downloads. Identical historical data is not guaranteed. The method name sgd_m denotes SoftServe-I, the normalized identity-metric control. PIDM runs 100k updates, but plots stop at 100k gradient evaluations, including replay. Plot results python plot.py outputs --task rnn --metric validation_mse \ --output outputs/rnn.pdf python plot.py outputs --task rnn --mode lr --metric selection_score \ --output outputs/rnn_lr.pdf Curves show means and seed min–max ranges; failed cohorts remain individual traces. For the standalone QME ablation, run python -m experiments.qme --output outputs/qme . Other options are available through --help . SoftServe preprint proposes quasi-Newton methods for deep learning

An arXiv preprint introduces SoftServe, a family of quasi-Newton methods for training neural networks. It describes diagonal and Kronecker-factored variants that use positive-definite curvature estimates and GPU-friendly Newton–Schulz iterations.

The authors report evaluations on recurrent networks, deep autoencoders, physics-informed neural networks and a 136-million-parameter physics-informed diffusion model, often achieving lower losses than Adam, Muon and SOAP. Those are results reported in the paper, not independently verified performance. The work is a research preprint; it reports no drone platform, sensors, payload, autonomous operation or deployment.
